### Corollary A.1 -- the proposed Dirichlet-dual Brown route is impossible

There is no finite function `C(d)` such that every measurable `Phi` and every phase-smooth
`0<=F<=1` obey

\[
 \left|\mathbb E_{\rm graph}F-\mathbb E_{\rm comp}F\right|
 \le C(d)\left(
   \operatorname{Var}_{\lambda}(F)
   +\int\|\nabla_\phi F\|_2^2d\lambda
 \right)^{1/2}.                                                           \tag{12}
\]

This remains false if the right side also contains any term that vanishes with the completed mean.

### Proof

Substitute `F_epsilon` from Theorem A into `(12)` and let `epsilon` tend to zero.  The left side
tends to one and the right side tends to zero. `square`

The corollary does not say that the actual circuit-incidence observable fails to mix.  It says its
mixing cannot follow from the parent's `O(r^2/D)` Dirichlet budget alone.

## 4. Every subcritical finite derivative hierarchy is blind

For an integer `k>=0`, define the conditional phase Sobolev quantity

\[
 \|F\|_{H^k_\phi(\lambda)}^2
 =\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}
   \int_{\Omega\times\mathbb T^d}
      |\partial_\phi^\alpha F|^2\,d\lambda.                              \tag{13}
\]

### Theorem B -- graph restriction requires half the phase codimension

If `2k<d`, the functions `(9)` satisfy

\[
 \boxed{
 \|F_\varepsilon\|_{H^k_\phi(\lambda)}^2
 \le C_{d,k,\eta}\sum_{j=0}^k\varepsilon^{d-2j}
 =O_{d,k,\eta}(\varepsilon^{d-2k})\longrightarrow0,}                    \tag{14}
\]

but their graph expectation is one.  Therefore restriction to the graph is not a bounded linear
functional on conditional phase `H^k` for any integer `k<d/2`.

### Proof

For every multi-index `alpha`, scaling `(8)` gives

\[
 \int_{\mathbb T^d}
   |\partial^\alpha g_\varepsilon|^2dm_d
 ={\varepsilon^{d-2|\alpha|}\over(2\pi)^d}
   \int_{\mathbb R^d}|\partial^\alpha\eta|^2.                            \tag{15}
\]

Translation by `Phi(omega)` does not change `(15)`.  Sum over `|alpha|<=k` and integrate over `mu`.
When `2k<d`, every exponent is positive and the largest derivative order dominates.  Equation `(5)`
then proves unboundedness of graph restriction. `square`

### Corollary B.1 -- many-body derivative-order barrier

For a `D`-dimensional state space, the projective spectral phase torus has `d=D-1` coordinates at
maximal projective rank.  A generic Sobolev-duality argument against the fixed-time graph therefore
cannot work with any integer derivative order

\[
 \boxed{k<{D-1\over2}.}                                                   \tag{16}
\]

For `n` qubits, `D=2^n`; every hierarchy of only `poly(n)` phase derivatives is subcritical.  In
particular, replacing the first-gradient estimate by finitely many higher gradients of order
`O(log n)` or `O(n)` does not repair the route.

This is a lower bound on a **generic restriction method**, not on the replica order required by the
physical shortcut event.  The parent theorem's `r=O(log n)` reporter remains exact; what fails is
the attempt to transfer it to a singular fixed-time graph using only generic phase smoothness.

## 5. Static-local specialization

Let `theta` denote the sampled coefficients of an ordinary time-independent local Hamiltonian and
let

\[
 \Phi_t(\theta)
 =t\big(E_2(\theta)-E_1(\theta),\ldots,
        E_D(\theta)-E_1(\theta)\big)\pmod {2\pi}.                         \tag{17}
\]

At fixed laboratory time `t`, the physical joint law of coefficients and phases is the graph law

\[
 \theta\longmapsto(\theta,\Phi_t(\theta)),                               \tag{18}
\]

whereas completed phase averaging replaces only the second coordinate by independent Haar phase.
Taking `Omega` to be the coefficient shell in Theorems A--B gives, without any spectral
regularity assumption:

1. graph observables can have physical expectation one and completed expectation tending to zero;
2. completed phase variance `O(r^2/D)` does not control their physical expectation;
3. no generic `poly(n)`-order phase Sobolev norm controls the restriction when `D=2^n`.

The obstruction is stronger than a dimension mismatch between coefficient space and phase space.
Conditioning on `theta` leaves a point mass in all `D-1` phase directions, so the relevant graph
codimension is the full projective phase dimension.

## 6. The opposite entropy trap: the physical image has a small arbitrary codebook

For `Γ = SL(2,ℤ)` the scattering matrix is `φ(s) = ξ(2s−1)/ξ(2s)` with `ξ(s) = π^{-s/2}Γ(s/2)ζ(s)`
(the identity `√π Γ(s−½)ζ(2s−1)/(Γ(s)ζ(2s))` rewritten). By Hadamard, `ξ'/ξ(s) = Σ_ρ 1/(s−ρ)`
(zeros paired symmetrically), hence

```text
−(1/4π) φ'/φ(½ + ir) = (1/2π) Σ_ρ [ 1/(1+2ir−ρ) − 1/(2ir−ρ) ]
                     = (1/2π) Σ_{ρ=β+iγ} [ (1−β)/((1−β)² + (2r−γ)²) + β/(β² + (2r−γ)²) ] =: Σ_ρ K_ρ(r),
```

the imaginary parts cancelling because `|φ(½+ir)| = 1` makes the left side real. Each `K_ρ ≥ 0`
is a pair of Poisson kernels in the variable `2r` centred at `γ`, of half-widths `β` and `1−β`,
total mass `∫ K_ρ dr = ½` independent of `β`, and peak `K_ρ(γ/2) = (1/2π)(1/β + 1/(1−β))`.
The trace formula (Iwaniec Thm 10.2, one cusp, area `π/3`) is

```text
Σ_j h(t_j) + Σ_ρ w_h(ρ) = G(h),   w_h(ρ) := ∫ h(r) K_ρ(r) dr,
```

with `G(h)` the identity, hyperbolic (prime-geodesic), elliptic and parabolic terms, all explicit
and RH-independent. The only created positivity in it is `Σ_j h(t_j) ≥ 0` for `h ≥ 0` on `ℝ`
(no exceptional eigenvalues for `SL(2,ℤ)`), and its only consequence for the zeros is the ledger
inequality `Σ_ρ w_h(ρ) ≤ G(h)`. Every other ingredient (Weyl's law with remainder, individual
eigenvalues) carries error terms of size `≫ r₀/log r₀` per unit of `‖h‖₁`, far above the `O(1)`
weight of a single zero, so it cannot isolate one zero.

**Theorem (Selberg-ledger ceiling).** Let `h ≥ 0` be admissible, `ρ₀ = β₀ + iγ₀` a zero with
`½ ≤ β₀ < 1`, and `Z` any set of zeros `ρ ≠ ρ₀` with `|γ − γ₀| ≤ 2`. Suppose `h` is supported in
`|r − γ₀/2| ≤ ¼`. Then

```text
w_h(ρ₀) ≤ (‖h‖₁/2π)(1/(1−β₀) + 1/β₀),        w_h(ρ) ≥ (2/29π) ‖h‖₁  for every ρ ∈ Z.
```

Consequently the ledger inequality `w_h(ρ₀) ≤ G(h) − Σ_{ρ∈Z} w_h(ρ)` can contradict the existence
of `ρ₀` only if `1/(1−β₀) + 1/β₀ > (4/29)|Z|`, i.e. only if `1 − β₀ < 29/(4|Z| − 58)`.

*Proof.* Upper bound: `K_{ρ₀}(r) ≤ K_{ρ₀}(γ₀/2)` pointwise since each Poisson kernel is maximal at
its centre; integrate against `h ≥ 0`. Lower bound: for `0 ≤ β ≤ 1`, `β² + (2r−γ)² ≤ 1 + (2r−γ)²`
and likewise for `1−β`, so `K_ρ(r) ≥ (1/2π)·(β + (1−β))/(1 + (2r−γ)²) = (1/2π)/(1+(2r−γ)²)`; on
the support of `h`, `|2r − γ| ≤ |2r − γ₀| + |γ₀ − γ| ≤ ½ + 2`, so `1 + (2r−γ)² ≤ 29/4`; integrate.
The consequence is the comparison `w_h(ρ₀) > Σ_Z w_h(ρ)` forced by `G(h) − Σ_Z w_h(ρ) ≥ Σ_{ρ∉Z} w_h(ρ) ≥ w_h(ρ₀)`
whenever `ρ₀` exists (all weights are nonnegative). ∎

Status: formalized (Lean, unconditional)

## Where this sits

`nyman-beurling-carrier-no-hardy-space.md` reduced the Riemann hypothesis, in Lean and unconditionally, to a
statement about `bdGram` — the Gram matrix of the Báez-Duarte generators — and nothing else. This card takes
the elementary part of `bdGram` as far as the technique goes and draws the boundary with a theorem rather
than a remark.

## What is proved

`RHTower/BaezDuarteGramReduction.lean`.

Expanding the diagonal square gives three tail integrals. Two collapse under the same dilation-and-split
identity that evaluated the target pairing:

* `integral_Ioc_fractSqInvSq` — `∫_θ^1 {v}²v^{-2}dv = 1 − θ`, because `{v}²v^{-2} = 1` on `(θ,1)`;
* `integral_Ioi_one_fractSq_dilate` — **`∫₁^∞ {θv}²v^{-2}dv = θ(1−θ) + θ·fractSqConst`**, where
  `fractSqConst = ∫₁^∞ {v}²v^{-2}dv`.

The third does not collapse: `fractCrossTail θ = ∫₁^∞ {θv}{v}v^{-2}dv` mixes two incommensurable dilations
and no substitution separates them. Result:

**`bdGram_self_eq` — `bdGram θ θ = θ(1−θ) + θ(1+θ)·fractSqConst − 2θ·fractCrossTail θ`.**

Also proved, and free from the earlier formulas: `explained_mass_le_one` — for *every* solution of a
Báez-Duarte normal system, `−∑ᵢ cᵢθᵢ log θᵢ ≤ 1`. This is `d² ≥ 0` plus the unit target, and it is an
unconditional constraint on the Gram systems that does not mention the zeros.

## The boundary, stated plainly

The diagonal is elementary modulo exactly two scalars:

1. `fractSqConst`, a single constant. It is a Stirling-type quantity (its interval-by-interval expansion is
   `∑ₙ [1 + n/(n+1) − 2n log(1+1/n)]`, convergent like `∑1/(3n²)`, whose closed form carries `log 2π`);
2. `fractCrossTail θ`, a function of `θ`. For rational `θ` this is the Vasyunin/cotangent-sum object.

Neither is reachable by dilation-and-split, which is the only technique that has worked in this lane —
every other computation here (`inner_bdGen_bdTarget`, the detector norms, the dilate transforms, the two
square terms above) fell to it, and these two provably do not, because the cross term has no single scaling
that normalises both fractional parts at once. Getting them needs new machinery: Mellin–Plancherel on a
half-line (mathlib has Fourier–Plancherel, but the transfer plus the boundary limit is a substantial build)
or the lattice/cotangent computation from scratch (mathlib has no Dedekind or cotangent sums).

That is the whole remaining gap between this corpus and a Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis via this
route — one constant and one function, both classical, neither cheap.

/-!
# The exponential limit of the spectral form factor

Under product Haar measure the normalized spectral form factor of a finite level set is a squared
character sum, so its moments are exactly the sums of squared multinomial coefficients: every
character with a nonzero index integrates to zero, and only the diagonal pairs of multiplicity
vectors survive.

Those moment constants converge to the factorials, which are the moments of the unit-mean
exponential law, and they never exceed the factorials, so the whole family carries one
factorial-geometric moment bound.  The method of moments therefore identifies the weak limit as the
unit-mean exponential law.
-/

open Filter MeasureTheory ProbabilityTheory Topology UnitAddTorus

namespace GaloisForLFunctions.HTGeometry

noncomputable section

section HaarMoments

private theorem fourier_one_pow (x : AddCircle (1 : ℝ)) (k : ℕ) :
    (fourier 1 x) ^ k = fourier (k : ℤ) x := by
  induction k with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
      rw [pow_succ, ih]
      have hcast : ((k + 1 : ℕ) : ℤ) = (k : ℤ) + 1 := by push_cast; ring
      rw [hcast, fourier_add]

theorem prod_mFourier_single_pow {D : ℕ} (p : Fin D → ℕ) (z : UnitAddTorus (Fin D)) :
    ∏ j : Fin D, (mFourier (Pi.single j (1 : ℤ)) z) ^ (p j) =
      mFourier (fun j => (p j : ℤ)) z := by
  have h1 : ∀ j : Fin D, mFourier (Pi.single j (1 : ℤ)) z = fourier 1 (z j) :=
    fun j => mFourier_single z j
  simp_rw [h1, fourier_one_pow]
  rfl

/-- The uniform phase sum on the product torus. -/
def torusPhaseSum (D : ℕ) (z : UnitAddTorus (Fin D)) : ℂ :=
  ∑ j : Fin D, mFourier (Pi.single j (1 : ℤ)) z

theorem torusPhaseSum_pow (D m : ℕ) (z : UnitAddTorus (Fin D)) :
    torusPhaseSum D z ^ m =
      ∑ p ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin D)).piAntidiag m,
        (Nat.multinomial Finset.univ p : ℂ) * mFourier (fun j => (p j : ℤ)) z := by
  rw [torusPhaseSum, Finset.sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun p _ => ?_
  rw [prod_mFourier_single_pow]

theorem continuous_torusPhaseSum (D : ℕ) : Continuous (torusPhaseSum D) := by
  refine continuous_finsetSum _ fun j _ => ?_
  exact (mFourier (Pi.single j (1 : ℤ))).continuous

/-- The normalized spectral form factor of a level set of prescribed size. -/
def torusSFF (D : ℕ) (z : UnitAddTorus (Fin D)) : ℝ := ‖torusPhaseSum D z‖ ^ 2 / D

theorem torusSFF_nonneg (D : ℕ) (z : UnitAddTorus (Fin D)) : 0 ≤ torusSFF D z := by
  rw [torusSFF]
  positivity

theorem continuous_torusSFF (D : ℕ) : Continuous (torusSFF D) :=
  ((continuous_torusPhaseSum D).norm.pow 2).div_const _

private theorem integrable_of_continuous {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X]
    [BorelSpace X] [CompactSpace X] {μ : Measure X} [IsFiniteMeasure μ]
    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f : X → E} (hf : Continuous f) :
    Integrable f μ :=
  hf.integrable_of_hasCompactSupport (HasCompactSupport.of_compactSpace f)

theorem ofReal_norm_sq (w : ℂ) : ((‖w‖ : ℝ) : ℂ) ^ 2 = w * (starRingEnd ℂ) w := by
  rw [Complex.mul_conj]
  norm_cast
  rw [Complex.normSq_eq_norm_sq]

/-- **Haar moments of the normalized spectral form factor.**  Every moment is the sum of squared
multinomial coefficients divided by the dimension raised to the replica order. -/
theorem integral_torusSFF_pow (D m : ℕ) :
    ∫ z : UnitAddTorus (Fin D), torusSFF D z ^ m
        ∂(finiteTorusHaarProbabilityMeasure (Fin D) :
          Measure (UnitAddTorus (Fin D))) = sffMoment D m := by
  classical
  set ν : Measure (UnitAddTorus (Fin D)) :=
    (finiteTorusHaarProbabilityMeasure (Fin D) : Measure (UnitAddTorus (Fin D))) with hν
  have hprob : IsProbabilityMeasure ν := by
    rw [hν]
    exact (finiteTorusHaarProbabilityMeasure (Fin D)).prop
  have hpoint : ∀ z : UnitAddTorus (Fin D), ((torusSFF D z ^ m : ℝ) : ℂ) =
      ∑ p ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin D)).piAntidiag m,
        ∑ q ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin D)).piAntidiag m,
          ((Nat.multinomial Finset.univ p : ℂ) * (Nat.multinomial Finset.univ q : ℂ) /
            (D : ℂ) ^ m) *
            mFourier ((fun j => (p j : ℤ)) + fun j => -(q j : ℤ)) z := by
    intro z
    have hA : ((torusSFF D z : ℝ) : ℂ) =
        torusPhaseSum D z * (starRingEnd ℂ) (torusPhaseSum D z) / (D : ℂ) := by
      rw [torusSFF]
      push_cast
      rw [ofReal_norm_sq]
    rw [show ((torusSFF D z ^ m : ℝ) : ℂ) = ((torusSFF D z : ℝ) : ℂ) ^ m by push_cast; ring, hA,
      div_pow, mul_pow, ← map_pow, torusPhaseSum_pow, map_sum]
    rw [Finset.sum_mul_sum, Finset.sum_div]
    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun p _ => ?_
    rw [Finset.sum_div]
    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun q _ => ?_
    rw [map_mul, Complex.conj_natCast, ← mFourier_neg]
    have hneg : (-(fun j => (q j : ℤ)) : Fin D → ℤ) = fun j => -(q j : ℤ) := rfl
    rw [hneg, mFourier_add]
    ring

# The flux identity with a source

The inhomogeneous clock equation `∂ₜ²u = Δu + Vu + f` has the same energy computation as the
homogeneous one, with one extra term: the source pairs with the time derivative. Everything else
cancels exactly as before, so

`∫ ∂ₜ(energy density) = 2∫ ((V+1)·u·∂ₜu + f·∂ₜu)`.

The extra pairing is what a Picard iteration on the Duhamel formula controls, so this identity is
the entry point to an existence proof by the energy method.
-/

def SolvesWaveEqSource (u V f : ℝ × (Fin d → ℝ) → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ p : ℝ × (Fin d → ℝ), waveDirDeriv (timeDir d) (waveDirDeriv (timeDir d) u) p
    = (∑ i : Fin d, waveDirDeriv (spaceDir d i) (waveDirDeriv (spaceDir d i) u) p)
      + V p * u p + f p

/-- A source-free solution is the special case of a vanishing source. -/
theorem solvesWaveEqSource_zero (h : SolvesWaveEq u V) :
    SolvesWaveEqSource u V (fun _ => 0) := by
  intro p
  rw [show ((fun _ : ℝ × (Fin d → ℝ) => (0 : ℝ)) p) = 0 from rfl, add_zero]
  exact h p

/-- **A source is absorbed into the potential wherever the field does not vanish**, so the
inhomogeneous equation is the homogeneous one for a modified potential off the zero set. -/

    {p : ℝ × (Fin d → ℝ)} (hp : u p ≠ 0) :
    waveDirDeriv (timeDir d) (waveDirDeriv (timeDir d) u) p
      = (∑ i : Fin d, waveDirDeriv (spaceDir d i) (waveDirDeriv (spaceDir d i) u) p)
        + (V p + f p / u p) * u p := by
  rw [h p]
  field_simp
  ring

/-!
# A quantitative Nyman–Beurling criterion, with explicit modulus

The three ingredients left open by the boundary/interior dichotomy assemble.

**(a) The space.**  Every Báez-Duarte generator is supported in `(0,1]`: for `t ≥ 1` both `1/t < 1`
and `θ/t < 1`, so `ρ_θ(t) = {θ/t} - θ{1/t} = θ/t - θ/t = 0`.  The target `1_{(0,1]}` is likewise
supported there.  The Mellin transform `f ↦ ∫₀¹ f(t)t^{-s}dt` therefore converges for `Re s < ½` and
maps `L²((0,1],dt)` unitarily onto the Hardy space `H²` of the half-plane `Re s < ½`, with the
Plancherel normalization

```text
‖f‖² = (1/2π) ∫_ℝ |f̂(½+iu)|² du ,
```

as the target itself confirms: `1̂(s) = 1/(1-s)`, whose boundary modulus squared integrates to `2π`,
matching `‖1_{(0,1]}‖² = 1`.

**(b) The vanishing constraint.**  The transform of a generator is `ζ(s)(n^{-s} - 1/n)/s`, so every
finite combination has transform `ζ(s)P(s)/s` with `P` entire.  At a zero `ρ` of `ζ` with `ρ ≠ 0`
this vanishes, and vanishing is preserved under `L²` limits because point evaluation in `H²` is
continuous.  The target does not vanish there: `1̂(ρ) = 1/(1-ρ) ≠ 0`.

**(c) The cost.**  With this normalization the diagonal kernel of `H²` of a half-plane is
`K(w,w) = 1/(2σ)`, `σ` the distance from `w` to the boundary line.  (The preceding module used the
unnormalized convention, where the constant is `1/(4πσ)`; the dichotomy is the same and only the
constant differs.)  The exact vanishing cost therefore gives, for a zero `ρ = β + iγ` of `ζ` with
`β < ½`,

```text
lim_N d_N  ≥  |1̂(ρ)| / √K(ρ,ρ)  =  √(1 - 2β) / |1 - ρ| .
```

By the functional equation the Riemann hypothesis fails exactly when such a `ρ` exists, so

> **If the Riemann hypothesis fails, the Báez-Duarte distances are bounded below by the explicit
> constant `√(1-2β)/|1-ρ|` for every zero `ρ` with `Re ρ < ½`.**

This is the quantitative form of the easy direction of the Nyman–Beurling criterion: not merely
`d_N ↛ 0`, but a modulus in the deviation.

**Universal height degradation.**  The constant is at most `1/|γ|`, since `√(1-2β) ≤ 1` and
`|1-ρ| ≥ |γ|`.  So a counterexample high up produces only a tiny floor, and combining the criterion
with numerical verification to height `X` would require the complementary analytic bound
`d_N ≤ 1/X` — with `d_N² ≍ 1/log N` that means `N ≥ exp(X²)`.  The same degradation appeared in the
flow lane, where verification to height `X` bounds `Λ` only by `π²/(2 log²X)`.  It is not an artefact
of either method:

> **Every quantified lane loses strength at a putative counterexample polynomially or exponentially
> in its height.  Numerical verification and analytic estimate never meet unless the analytic
> estimate is itself as strong as the verification height.**

That is the unified reason the "verify below, estimate above" architecture stalls, and it applies to
the Nyman–Beurling lane exactly as it does to the de Bruijn–Newman lane.

This file formalizes the kernel with the correct normalization, the explicit floor, and the height
degradation.
-/

open Real

noncomputable section

namespace RHTower

/-- The diagonal reproducing kernel of `H²` of a half-plane in the Plancherel normalization
`‖F‖² = (1/2π)∫|F|²`. -/
def nymanBeurlingHardyKernel (sigma : ℝ) : ℝ := 1 / (2 * sigma)

/-- **The explicit floor.**  The cost of vanishing at a point at distance `σ` from the boundary, for
a target of modulus `m` there, is `m·√(2σ)`. -/
def nbFloor (m sigma : ℝ) : ℝ := m * Real.sqrt (2 * sigma)

/-- The floor is the target modulus divided by the square root of the diagonal kernel. -/
theorem nbFloor_eq {m sigma : ℝ} (hs : 0 < sigma) :
    nbFloor m sigma = m / Real.sqrt (nymanBeurlingHardyKernel sigma) := by
  unfold nbFloor nymanBeurlingHardyKernel
  have hpos : (0 : ℝ) < 2 * sigma := by positivity
  rw [one_div, Real.sqrt_inv, div_inv_eq_mul]

/-- **Positivity.**  A zero strictly off the critical line gives a strictly positive floor. -/
theorem nbFloor_pos {m sigma : ℝ} (hm : 0 < m) (hs : 0 < sigma) : 0 < nbFloor m sigma := by
  unfold nbFloor
  have : 0 < Real.sqrt (2 * sigma) := Real.sqrt_pos.mpr (by positivity)
  positivity

/-- **The floor in terms of the zero.**  With `σ = ½ - β` and `m = 1/|1-ρ|`, the floor is
`√(1-2β)/|1-ρ|`. -/
theorem nbFloor_of_zero (beta r : ℝ) :
    nbFloor (1 / r) (1 / 2 - beta) = Real.sqrt (1 - 2 * beta) / r := by
  unfold nbFloor
  have h2 : 2 * (1 / 2 - beta) = 1 - 2 * beta := by ring
  rw [h2, one_div, inv_mul_eq_div]

/-- **Height degradation.**  Since `√(1-2β) ≤ 1` for `β ≥ 0` and `|1-ρ| ≥ |γ|`, the floor is at most
`1/|γ|`: a counterexample high up gives only a tiny floor. -/
theorem nbFloor_le_inv_height {beta r g : ℝ} (hb0 : 0 ≤ beta)
    (hg : 0 < g) (hr : g ≤ r) :
    Real.sqrt (1 - 2 * beta) / r ≤ 1 / g := by
  have hrpos : 0 < r := lt_of_lt_of_le hg hr
  have hle : Real.sqrt (1 - 2 * beta) ≤ 1 := by
    have h1 : 1 - 2 * beta ≤ 1 := by linarith

/-!
# A perturbed oscillator in a general phase parameterization

The energy method for `w'' + (1 + q) w = 0` needs no privileged variable.  If `φ` is an increasing
phase and derivatives with respect to `φ` are written `Dw = w'/φ'`, `DDw = (Dw)'/φ'`, the same
three facts hold with `φ'` decorating each derivative:

```text
E = w² + (Dw)²,        E' = -2 φ' q w Dw,
A = w cos φ - Dw sin φ,   A' =  φ' q w sin φ,
B = w sin φ + Dw cos φ,   B' = -φ' q w cos φ.
```

If the perturbation obeys `|q| ≤ κ/φ²` then `E exp(κ/φ)` is antitone, because the drift integrates
to `∫ φ' κ/φ² = κ/φ`.

Working in the phase parameterization rather than in the phase variable avoids inverting `φ`
altogether: every statement is about functions of the original variable, and the change of
variables never has to be performed.
-/

noncomputable section

open Set

namespace GaloisForLFunctions.HTGeometry

variable {w Dw DDw q φ Dφ : ℝ → ℝ}

/-- The oscillator energy in a phase parameterization. -/
def phaseEnergy (w Dw : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ := w x ^ 2 + Dw x ^ 2

theorem phaseEnergy_nonneg (w Dw : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : 0 ≤ phaseEnergy w Dw x := by
  rw [phaseEnergy]
  positivity

/-- **The energy is almost conserved.**  The unperturbed contribution cancels exactly; what is left
is the perturbation times the phase speed. -/
theorem hasDerivAt_phaseEnergy {x : ℝ}
    (hw : HasDerivAt w (Dφ x * Dw x) x) (hDw : HasDerivAt Dw (Dφ x * DDw x) x)
    (hode : DDw x + (1 + q x) * w x = 0) :
    HasDerivAt (phaseEnergy w Dw) (-(2 * Dφ x * q x * (w x * Dw x))) x := by
  have h1 : HasDerivAt (fun v : ℝ => w v ^ 2) (2 * w x * (Dφ x * Dw x)) x := by
    have h := hw.pow 2
    have hv : ((2 : ℕ) : ℝ) * w x ^ (2 - 1) * (Dφ x * Dw x)
        = 2 * w x * (Dφ x * Dw x) := by norm_num
    rw [hv] at h
    exact h
  have h2 : HasDerivAt (fun v : ℝ => Dw v ^ 2) (2 * Dw x * (Dφ x * DDw x)) x := by
    have h := hDw.pow 2
    have hv : ((2 : ℕ) : ℝ) * Dw x ^ (2 - 1) * (Dφ x * DDw x)
        = 2 * Dw x * (Dφ x * DDw x) := by norm_num
    rw [hv] at h
    exact h
  have h := h1.add h2
  have hval : 2 * w x * (Dφ x * Dw x) + 2 * Dw x * (Dφ x * DDw x)
      = -(2 * Dφ x * q x * (w x * Dw x)) := by
    have hsec : DDw x = -((1 + q x) * w x) := by linarith
    rw [hsec]
    ring
  rw [hval] at h
  exact h

/-- **The differential inequality**, by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. -/
theorem abs_deriv_phaseEnergy_le {x κ : ℝ} (hDφ : 0 ≤ Dφ x)
    (hq : |q x| ≤ κ / φ x ^ 2) :
    |-(2 * Dφ x * q x * (w x * Dw x))| ≤ Dφ x * (κ / φ x ^ 2) * phaseEnergy w Dw x := by
  have hamgm : 2 * |w x| * |Dw x| ≤ w x ^ 2 + Dw x ^ 2 := by
    nlinarith [sq_nonneg (|w x| - |Dw x|), sq_abs (w x), sq_abs (Dw x)]
  have hκ : (0 : ℝ) ≤ κ / φ x ^ 2 := le_trans (abs_nonneg _) hq
  rw [abs_neg, abs_mul, abs_mul, abs_mul, phaseEnergy, abs_mul (w x) (Dw x),
    abs_of_nonneg hDφ]
  have habs : |(2 : ℝ)| = 2 := by norm_num
  rw [habs]
  have hnn : (0 : ℝ) ≤ |w x| * |Dw x| := by positivity
  calc 2 * Dφ x * |q x| * (|w x| * |Dw x|)
      ≤ 2 * Dφ x * (κ / φ x ^ 2) * (|w x| * |Dw x|) := by
        have := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hq (by positivity : (0 : ℝ) ≤ 2 * Dφ x)
        nlinarith [hnn]
    _ ≤ Dφ x * (κ / φ x ^ 2) * (w x ^ 2 + Dw x ^ 2) := by
        nlinarith [hamgm, mul_nonneg hDφ hκ]

/-- The cosine coefficient against the unperturbed basis in the phase. -/
def phaseCosCoeff (w Dw φ : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ := w x * Real.cos (φ x) - Dw x * Real.sin (φ x)

/-- The sine coefficient. -/
def phaseSinCoeff (w Dw φ : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ := w x * Real.sin (φ x) + Dw x * Real.cos (φ x)

/-- **The exact two-branch representation.** -/
theorem phase_eq_coeff (w Dw φ : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) :
    w x = phaseCosCoeff w Dw φ x * Real.cos (φ x)
      + phaseSinCoeff w Dw φ x * Real.sin (φ x) := by
  rw [phaseCosCoeff, phaseSinCoeff]
  linear_combination (-(w x)) * Real.sin_sq_add_cos_sq (φ x)

/-- The coefficients carry exactly the energy. -/
theorem phaseCoeff_sq_add (w Dw φ : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) :
    phaseCosCoeff w Dw φ x ^ 2 + phaseSinCoeff w Dw φ x ^ 2 = phaseEnergy w Dw x := by
  rw [phaseCosCoeff, phaseSinCoeff, phaseEnergy]
  nlinarith [Real.sin_sq_add_cos_sq (φ x)]

theorem hasDerivAt_phaseCosCoeff {x : ℝ}
    (hφ : HasDerivAt φ (Dφ x) x)
    (hw : HasDerivAt w (Dφ x * Dw x) x) (hDw : HasDerivAt Dw (Dφ x * DDw x) x)
    (hode : DDw x + (1 + q x) * w x = 0) :
    HasDerivAt (phaseCosCoeff w Dw φ) (Dφ x * q x * w x * Real.sin (φ x)) x := by
  have hc : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => Real.cos (φ t)) (-Real.sin (φ x) * Dφ x) x :=
    (Real.hasDerivAt_cos (φ x)).comp x hφ
  have hs : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => Real.sin (φ t)) (Real.cos (φ x) * Dφ x) x :=

/-!
# Polynomial moments of literal coprime deletion polygons

For actual moduli `P=p+1` and `Q=q+1`, join the successive prefix endpoints
`(n mod P,n mod Q)` by straight segments. Their velocities are exactly the existing
Euler-deletion coefficients, and one common period is a closed polygon.

CRT factors every polynomial segment density into two explicit one-coordinate phase sums.
All coefficient-degree-at-most-three polynomial one-forms have zero circulation. The
higher moment `integral x*y^3 dx` is exactly `P*(P-1)*Q*(Q-1)*(Q-2)/120` for coprime
`P,Q`. In particular the literal moduli-2-and-3 path gives the closed value `1/10`.

This is a finite unweighted arithmetic statement. It supplies no assertion about a weighted
infinite product, no vanishing at a zeta zero, and no RH implication. Polynomial-moment
and path-signature methods have published ancestry; no global novelty claim is made here.
-/

open scoped BigOperators
namespace RHTower.DeletionJointPolygon
noncomputable section

/-- Velocity of the literal modulus `p+1` deletion path. -/
def velocity (p n : ℕ) : ℝ := blockDeletionCoefficient (p+1) (n+1)

/-- Straight interpolation of the exact residue-valued prefix. -/
def position (p n : ℕ) (t : ℝ) : ℝ := (n % (p+1) : ℕ) + t * velocity p n

/-- Polynomial one-form integrated along one full common period. -/
def circulation (p q a b : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ t in (0:ℝ)..1, ∑ n ∈ Finset.range ((p+1)*(q+1)),
    position p n t ^ a * position q n t ^ b * velocity p n

/-- Position moments across one coordinate's phases. -/
def phaseMoment (p k : ℕ) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ j ∈ Finset.range p, ((j:ℝ)+t)^k) + ((p:ℝ)*(1-t))^k

/-- Velocity-weighted position moments across one coordinate's phases. -/
def velocityMoment (p k : ℕ) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ j ∈ Finset.range p, ((j:ℝ)+t)^k) - (p:ℝ)*((p:ℝ)*(1-t))^k

theorem velocity_of_lt {p n : ℕ} (hn : n < p) : velocity p n = 1 := by
  have hd : ¬ p+1 ∣ n+1 := Nat.not_dvd_of_pos_of_lt (Nat.succ_pos n)
    (Nat.succ_lt_succ hn)
  simp [velocity, blockDeletionCoefficient, hd]

theorem velocity_last (p : ℕ) : velocity p p = -(p:ℝ) := by
  simp [velocity, blockDeletionCoefficient]

theorem position_of_lt {p n : ℕ} (hn : n < p) (t : ℝ) :
    position p n t = (n:ℝ)+t := by
  simp [position, Nat.mod_eq_of_lt (Nat.lt_succ_of_lt hn), velocity_of_lt hn]

theorem position_last (p : ℕ) (t : ℝ) : position p p t = (p:ℝ)*(1-t) := by
  simp only [position, Nat.mod_eq_of_lt (Nat.lt_succ_self p), velocity_last]
  ring

theorem velocity_periodic (p : ℕ) : Function.Periodic (velocity p) (p+1) := by
  intro n
  exact congrArg (fun z : ℤ => (z:ℝ))
    (DeletionCoprimeWords.shifted_deletion_periodic (p+1) n)

theorem position_periodic (p : ℕ) (t : ℝ) :
    Function.Periodic (fun n => position p n t) (p+1) := by
  intro n
  simp only [position, Nat.add_mod_right, velocity_periodic p n]

theorem sum_position_pow (p k : ℕ) (t : ℝ) :
    (∑ n ∈ Finset.range (p+1), position p n t ^ k) = phaseMoment p k t := by
  rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, position_last]
  unfold phaseMoment
  congr 1
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun n hn => by rw [position_of_lt (Finset.mem_range.mp hn)])

theorem sum_position_pow_velocity (p k : ℕ) (t : ℝ) :
    (∑ n ∈ Finset.range (p+1), position p n t ^ k * velocity p n) =
      velocityMoment p k t := by
  rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, position_last, velocity_last]
  unfold velocityMoment
  have hs : (∑ n ∈ Finset.range p, position p n t ^ k * velocity p n) =
      ∑ n ∈ Finset.range p, ((n:ℝ)+t)^k := by
    apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
    intro n hn
    rw [position_of_lt (Finset.mem_range.mp hn), velocity_of_lt (Finset.mem_range.mp hn), mul_one]
  rw [hs]
  ring

/-- The starting coordinate is the actual sum of previous deletion jumps. -/
theorem position_zero_eq_prefix (p n : ℕ) :
    position p n 0 = (deletionCoeffPartialSum (p+1) n : ℝ) := by
  simp only [position, zero_mul, add_zero, deletionCoeffPartialSum_eq_mod, Int.cast_natCast]

/-- Consecutive straight segments meet at their endpoints. -/
theorem segment_endpoint (p n : ℕ) : position p n 1 = position p (n+1) 0 := by
  have h : deletionCoeffPartialSum (p+1) n + blockDeletionCoefficient (p+1) (n+1) =
      deletionCoeffPartialSum (p+1) (n+1) := by
    exact (Finset.sum_range_succ _ _).symm
  rw [deletionCoeffPartialSum_eq_mod, deletionCoeffPartialSum_eq_mod] at h
  have hr := congrArg (fun z : ℤ => (z:ℝ)) h
  simpa only [position, velocity, one_mul, zero_mul, add_zero, Int.cast_add, Int.cast_natCast] using hr

/-- A common period returns both literal coordinates to the origin. -/
theorem common_period_closed (p q : ℕ) :
    position p ((p+1)*(q+1)) 0 = 0 ∧ position q ((p+1)*(q+1)) 0 = 0 := by
  simp [position]

/-- CRT factors the actual segment integrand; no averaging approximation is used. -/

noncomputable def deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy
    (p : Nat.Primes) (f : DeningerPrimePacketComplexHaarL2 p) : ℝ :=
  deningerTateCircleModeRate 1 *
    ‖deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstMode p f‖ ^ 2

/-- Exact first-mode energy: the Tate-normalized eigenvalue is the prime-independent `2π`. -/
theorem deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy_eq
    (p : Nat.Primes) (f : DeningerPrimePacketComplexHaarL2 p) :
    deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy p f =
      (2 * Real.pi) * ‖f‖ ^ 2 := by
  rw [deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy,
    norm_deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstMode]
  simp [deningerTateCircleModeRate]

/-- Every nonzero packet coefficient acquires strictly positive first-mode Tate energy. -/
theorem deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy_pos
    (p : Nat.Primes) {f : DeningerPrimePacketComplexHaarL2 p}
    (hf : f ≠ 0) :

  rw [deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy_eq]

    (sq_pos_of_pos (norm_pos_iff.mpr hf))

/-- Complex pullback of a finite packet function to the literal profinite packet. -/
def deningerPrimeFiniteStageComplexPullback (p : Nat.Primes)
    (s : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStage (p : ℕ))
    (F : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStageQuotient (p : ℕ) s → ℂ) :
    C(DeningerPacketFrobeniusQuotient p, ℂ) where
  toFun x := F (deningerPrimeFiniteStageQuotientReduction p s x)
  continuous_toFun :=
    continuous_of_discreteTopology.comp
      (deningerPrimeFiniteStageQuotientReduction_continuous p s)

/-- Finite packet function in complex packet Haar `L²`. -/
def deningerPrimeFiniteStageComplexHaarL2 (p : Nat.Primes)
    (s : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStage (p : ℕ))
    (F : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStageQuotient (p : ℕ) s → ℂ) :
    DeningerPrimePacketComplexHaarL2 p :=
  ContinuousMap.toLp 2 (deningerPrimePacketHaarMeasure p) ℂ
    (deningerPrimeFiniteStageComplexPullback p s F)

/-- Canonical first suspension mode of a finite packet function. -/
def deningerPrimeFiniteStageFirstSuspensionMode (p : Nat.Primes)
    (s : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStage (p : ℕ))
    (F : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStageQuotient (p : ℕ) s → ℂ) :
    DeningerPrimeSuspensionHaarL2 p :=
  deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstMode p
    (deningerPrimeFiniteStageComplexHaarL2 p s F)

/-- A nonzero finite packet function gives a nonzero first suspension mode. -/
theorem deningerPrimeFiniteStageFirstSuspensionMode_ne_zero
    (p : Nat.Primes) (s : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStage (p : ℕ))
    {F : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStageQuotient (p : ℕ) s → ℂ}
    (hF : F ≠ 0) :
    deningerPrimeFiniteStageFirstSuspensionMode p s F ≠ 0 := by
  intro hmode
  have hLp : deningerPrimeFiniteStageComplexHaarL2 p s F = 0 := by
    apply deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstMode_injective p
    rw [map_zero]
    exact hmode
  have hzero : deningerPrimeFiniteStageComplexPullback p s F = 0 := by
    apply ContinuousMap.toLp_injective
      (𝕜 := ℂ) (p := 2) (E := ℂ)
      (deningerPrimePacketHaarMeasure p)
    rw [map_zero]
    exact hLp
  apply hF
  funext q
  obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ :=
    deningerPrimeFiniteStageQuotientReduction_surjective p s q
  have hpoint := DFunLike.congr_fun hzero x
  change F (deningerPrimeFiniteStageQuotientReduction p s x) = 0 at hpoint
  simpa [hx] using hpoint

/-- A nonzero finite packet function has strictly positive first-mode Tate energy. -/
theorem deningerPrimeFiniteStageFirstSuspensionMode_energy_pos
    (p : Nat.Primes) (s : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStage (p : ℕ))
    {F : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStageQuotient (p : ℕ) s → ℂ}
    (hF : F ≠ 0) :
    0 < deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy p
      (deningerPrimeFiniteStageComplexHaarL2 p s F) := by
  apply deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy_pos
  intro hzero
  apply deningerPrimeFiniteStageFirstSuspensionMode_ne_zero p s hF
  change deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstMode p
      (deningerPrimeFiniteStageComplexHaarL2 p s F) = 0
  rw [hzero, map_zero]

/-- **Actual Wrat first-mode admission.**  Every nonzero finite packet function has both a fixed
rational-Witt witness and a nonzero positive-energy first suspension mode on the literal prime
fibre. -/
theorem deningerPrimeComplexifiedRationalWitt_exists_nonzero_firstSuspensionMode
    (p : Nat.Primes) (s : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStage (p : ℕ))
    (F : DeningerFiniteFrobeniusStageQuotient (p : ℕ) s → ℂ)
    (hF : F ≠ 0) :
    ∃ w : DeningerFiniteCyclotomicWittAlgebra s.modulus,
      deningerPrimeComplexifiedRationalWittFrobenius p
          (deningerPrimeFiniteCyclotomicWittInclusion p s w) =
        deningerPrimeFiniteCyclotomicWittInclusion p s w ∧
      (∀ u : (ZMod s.modulus)ˣ,
        deningerFiniteCyclotomicWittEvaluation s.modulus u w =
          F (QuotientGroup.mk u)) ∧
      deningerPrimeFiniteStageFirstSuspensionMode p s F ≠ 0 ∧
      0 < deningerPrimeSuspensionFirstModeGreenEnergy p

This module packages the first nonzero arithmetic gap-moment defect at a

* completed xi symmetry gives an exact relation between the defects at

* the first omitted eta interval gives an explicit strict saving over the

The result is an exact completion-weighted norm ratio and unconditional

/-!
# Cofinal discharge of the Gamma second-subprincipal reflection

The branchwise second-subprincipal order theorem needs principal cancellation, first-partial
cancellation, and a nonzero complete second boundary on one common Gamma pole branch.  This module
represents that complete three-term boundary in the existing faithful Laurent algebra generated by
the factorial scale and positive derivatives of the regular Gamma pole unit.

The symbols for `R₀'(0)` and `R₁(0)` both use the second positive unit derivative, with the exact
factor `1/2`; `R₁(0)` additionally carries one inverse physical scale.  Together with the existing
finite-part symbol for `R₀(0)`, they produce one symbolic source for the full second boundary.
Joint Laurent injectivity turns symbolic nonvanishing into a nonzero boundary germ.  Eventual
principal and first-partial cancellations can then be intersected with a nonzero boundary value
beyond any prescribed branch bound, yielding simultaneous exact order `-(W-2)` for covariant and
native affine Gamma packets.

Two specializations of the positive unit-derivative variables isolate the surviving `X₁` and
`X₀²` channels.  After first-partial cancellation this gives an exact classification: the complete
second symbol is nonzero precisely when the first-jet partial reflection or repeated-base Hessian
reflection is nonzero.  Thus the final cofinal theorem needs only intrinsic principal-reflection
conditions, not an opaque nonzero boundary combination.
-/

open Complex Filter Topology Finset MvPolynomial Polynomial LaurentPolynomial

namespace GaloisForLFunctions

noncomputable section

local instance gammaPoleWeightedSecondSubprincipalCofinalLocalInst1 : Algebra ℂ NatGerm := complexNatGerm.toAlgebra

/-- Laurent symbol for the center derivative `R₀'(0)` of the base Gamma regular remainder. -/
def gammaPoleBaseRemainderDerivativeSymbol :
    GammaPoleScaleDerivativeSymbolic :=
  -(gammaPoleComplexScaleDerivativeInclude (2 : ℂ)⁻¹ *
    LaurentPolynomial.C
      (MvPolynomial.X 1 : MvPolynomial ℕ GammaPoleRationalBase))

/-- Laurent symbol for the first regular value `R₁(0)`; it carries one inverse factorial scale. -/
def gammaPoleFirstJetRemainderSymbol :
    GammaPoleScaleDerivativeSymbolic :=
  LaurentPolynomial.T (-1) *
    gammaPoleComplexScaleDerivativeInclude (2 : ℂ)⁻¹ *
    LaurentPolynomial.C
      (MvPolynomial.X 1 : MvPolynomial ℕ GammaPoleRationalBase)

/-- The base-remainder derivative symbol evaluates to the first finite-part jet germ. -/
theorem eval_baseRemainderDerivativeSymbol :
    gammaPoleScaleAndUnitDerivativeLaurentEval
        gammaPoleBaseRemainderDerivativeSymbol =
      gammaPoleFinitePartJetGerm 1 := by
  rw [gammaPoleBaseRemainderDerivativeSymbol, map_neg, map_mul]
  have hscalar : gammaPoleScaleAndUnitDerivativeLaurentEval
      (gammaPoleComplexScaleDerivativeInclude (2 : ℂ)⁻¹) =

# Local physical-jet to completed Hellinger--Gamma incidence bridge

The internally promoted Möbius--theta source retains the first nonzero Xi
jet at every divisor support, including arbitrary multiplicity.  This file
uses that source coefficient as the coefficient of the canonical completed
Calderón--Witt incidence vector at the first multiplicity copy.

The resulting completed incidence is nonzero, decodes to the same physical
source coefficient times the actual Gamma incidence witness, and is
recovered by the completed Hellinger--Gamma adjacent coface for every real
modular displacement.  Thus physical-jet provenance and Hodge-incidence
provenance meet coefficient-faithfully at every local divisor block.

This is the local joint marginal required by conservative resolved graph
descent.  It does not assert the missing global closed-graph grade
separation: raw coface recovery still holds both on and off the critical
line.
-/

/-- First multiplicity copy of a divisor support. -/
def thetaInternalJetLeadingZeroCopy (rho : XiDivisorSupport) : XiZeroCopy :=
  ⟨rho, ⟨0, xiSupportMultiplicity_pos rho⟩⟩

/-- Diagonal physical source moment at the first nonzero Xi jet order. -/
def thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient (rho : XiDivisorSupport) : ℂ :=
  thetaInternalJetLocalMomentMatrix rho
    ⟨0, xiSupportMultiplicity_pos rho⟩
    ⟨0, xiSupportMultiplicity_pos rho⟩

/-- The leading physical source coefficient is the first nonzero Xi jet. -/
theorem thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient_eq (rho : XiDivisorSupport) :
    thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient rho =
      iteratedDeriv (xiSupportMultiplicity rho) XiC
        (xiSpectralPointSupport rho) := by
  exact thetaInternalJetLocalMomentMatrix_diag rho _

/-- The leading physical source coefficient never vanishes. -/
theorem thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient_ne_zero (rho : XiDivisorSupport) :
    thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient rho ≠ 0 := by
  rw [thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient_eq]
  exact iteratedDeriv_XiC_ne_zero_at_supportMultiplicity rho

/-- The canonical completed incidence vector has normalized coefficient one. -/
theorem deningerCanonicalCompletedIncidenceVector_coefficient
    (p q : Nat.Primes) (hpq : p ≠ q) (r : XiZeroCopy) :
    deningerCalderonWittCrossPrimeXiIncidenceCompletionCoefficient p q hpq r
        (deningerCanonicalCompletedIncidenceVector p q hpq r) = 1 := by
  have h := congrArg
    (deningerCalderonWittCrossPrimeNormalizedIncidenceCoordinate p q hpq)
    (deningerCanonicalCompletedIncidenceVector_sourceValue p q hpq r)
  simpa [deningerCalderonWittCrossPrimeXiIncidenceCompletionSourceValue,
    deningerCalderonWittCrossPrimeNormalizedIncidenceCoordinate_witness] using h

/-- Completed incidence carrying the first nonzero physical theta-source jet. -/
def thetaInternalJetLeadingCompletedIncidence
    (p q : Nat.Primes) (hpq : p ≠ q) (rho : XiDivisorSupport) :
    DeningerCalderonWittCrossPrimeXiIncidenceCompletion p q hpq :=
  thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient rho •
    deningerCanonicalCompletedIncidenceVector p q hpq
      (thetaInternalJetLeadingZeroCopy rho)

/-- The chosen completed incidence coefficient is exactly the physical source moment. -/
theorem thetaInternalJetLeadingCompletedIncidence_coefficient
    (p q : Nat.Primes) (hpq : p ≠ q) (rho : XiDivisorSupport) :
    deningerCalderonWittCrossPrimeXiIncidenceCompletionCoefficient p q hpq
        (thetaInternalJetLeadingZeroCopy rho)
        (thetaInternalJetLeadingCompletedIncidence p q hpq rho) =
      thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient rho := by
  rw [thetaInternalJetLeadingCompletedIncidence, map_smul,
    deningerCanonicalCompletedIncidenceVector_coefficient]
  simp

/-- No local physical multiplicity direction disappears in completed incidence. -/
theorem thetaInternalJetLeadingCompletedIncidence_ne_zero
    (p q : Nat.Primes) (hpq : p ≠ q) (rho : XiDivisorSupport) :
    thetaInternalJetLeadingCompletedIncidence p q hpq rho ≠ 0 := by
  intro hzero
  have hcoefficient := congrArg
    (deningerCalderonWittCrossPrimeXiIncidenceCompletionCoefficient p q hpq
      (thetaInternalJetLeadingZeroCopy rho)) hzero
  rw [thetaInternalJetLeadingCompletedIncidence_coefficient, map_zero] at hcoefficient
  exact thetaInternalJetLeadingSourceCoefficient_ne_zero rho hcoefficient

/-!
### Constructing a normed space structure from an inner product

In the definition of an inner product space, we require the existence of a norm, which is equal
(but maybe not defeq) to the square root of the scalar product. This makes it possible to put
an inner product space structure on spaces with a preexisting norm (for instance `ℝ`), with good
properties. However, sometimes, one would like to define the norm starting only from a well-behaved
scalar product. This is what we implement in this paragraph, starting from a structure
`InnerProductSpace.Core` stating that we have a nice scalar product.

Our goal here is not to develop a whole theory with all the supporting API, as this will be done
below for `InnerProductSpace`. Instead, we implement the bare minimum to go as directly as
possible to the construction of the norm and the proof of the triangular inequality.

Warning: Do not use this `Core` structure if the space you are interested in already has a norm
instance defined on it, otherwise this will create a second non-defeq norm instance!
-/

source_arguments.name: RHTower.infDist_span_eq_norm_starProjection_orthogonal
source_arguments.statement:
theorem infDist_span_eq_norm_starProjection_orthogonal (S : Set H) (x : H) :
    Metric.infDist x (Submodule.span 𝕜 S : Set H)
      = ‖(Submodule.span 𝕜 S)ᗮ.starProjection x‖
source_arguments.source_statement:
theorem infDist_span_eq_norm_starProjection_orthogonal (S : Set H) (x : H) :
    Metric.infDist x (Submodule.span 𝕜 S : Set H)
      = ‖(Submodule.span 𝕜 S)ᗮ.starProjection x‖
source_arguments.proof_excerpt:
by
  set K := Submodule.span 𝕜 S with hKdef
  set P := Kᗮ.starProjection x with hPdef
  have hPmem : P ∈ Kᗮ := Submodule.starProjection_apply_mem _ x
  have hsub : x - P ∈ Kᗮᗮ := Submodule.sub_starProjection_mem_orthogonal x
  have hclos : x - P ∈ K.topologicalClosure := by
    rwa [Submodule.orthogonal_orthogonal_eq_closure] at hsub
  refine le_antisymm ?_ ?_
  · have h1 : Metric.infDist x (K.topologicalClosure : Set H) ≤ ‖P‖ := by
      have h := Metric.infDist_le_dist_of_mem (x := x) (SetLike.mem_coe.2 hclos)
      rwa [dist_eq_norm, sub_sub_cancel] at h
    rwa [Submodule.topologicalClosure_coe, Metric.infDist_closure] at h1
  · rcases eq_or_ne P 0 with h0 | hne
    · rw [h0, norm_zero]
      exact Metric.infDist_nonneg
    · have hppos : 0 < ‖P‖ := norm_pos_iff.mpr hne
      have hbound := norm_inner_le_norm_mul_infDist_span S x P
        ((mem_orthogonal_span_iff S P).1 hPmem)
      rw [inner_starProjection_orthogonal_self K x, RCLike.norm_ofReal,
        abs_of_nonneg (by positivity : (0 : ℝ) ≤ ‖P‖ ^ 2), sq] at hbound
      exact le_of_mul_le_mul_left hbound hppos

/-- **The bound is attained.**  Some vector orthogonal to the family, of norm at most one, pairs with the
target exactly at the distance: the detector method is exact. -/

prose.text:
# CCM-FU: complete binary gcd compensation

- **Stage:** 1-in-progress
- **Type:** [BRIDGE], direct signed-source proof candidate.
- **Goal:** Complete signed Abel bound, CCM-FU boundary chain, RH.
- **Parent:** [complete reserve-extension attack](ccm-fu-reserve-extension-induction.md).

Write `G_r(M)` for the exact ordered off-diagonal contribution of channel
pairs with gcd r. The corpus proves
`sum_r G_r(M)=S(M)^2-Q_empty(M)`, while individual components can be positive.
The complete coprime-column cancellation theorem suggests retaining a whole
prime-incidence packet before taking a sign or absolute value. Its floor
weights cannot simply be replaced by the divisor Abel weights: that would
discard the actual source dependence.

This attempt tests the concrete binary packet

`J_r(M)=G_r(M)+G_(2r)(M)`, for positive odd r.

The frozen sufficient claim is `J_r(M)<=0` at every cutoff and every positive
odd r. Every nonzero gcd component has squarefree gcd, because a repeated
prime in the gcd makes both Möbius coefficients zero. Thus grouping by odd
part gives the complete off-diagonal as `sum_(r odd) J_r(M)`. If the proposed
sign is true, it gives SD1 directly, followed by the already proved quadratic
diagonal ceiling and the full CCM-FU RH receiver. This candidate does not
assume a safe prime-elimination order or omit the terminal source square.

The choice of 2 fixes the smallest-prime incidence pair, without fitted
weights. The known positive primitive component at cutoff eleven does not
decide the sign of its complete binary packet. No claim that this packet
sign follows from unsigned positivity is made.

## Frozen discriminating test

Use every saved gcd component at every cutoff 1 through 100 in
`2-fully-proven/computations/ccm-fu-gcd-cross-sign-2026-09-06/components.csv`.
Do not regenerate those channels or extend the cutoff range. Check every
odd r<=M, interpreting G_(2r)=0 outside the cutoff. Use tolerance
`1e-12*max(1,abs(total_off_diagonal))`, retain every failure and every packet,
and check that their complete sum reconstructs the saved off-diagonal.

Independently reconstruct the first failing cutoff from the defining
logarithmic factorial, divisor sum, Möbius coefficients and Abel weights at
80 decimal digits. Retain every component and channel there. A failed
packet refutes this sufficient proof candidate at the numerical-evidence
level; it does not refute SD1, the complete reserve-extension claim, or RH.
A pass leaves the universal arithmetic packet sign to prove.

Execute only on RunPod, with at most eight cutoff workers and a 60-second
foreground deadline. Download the exact script, input hash, output and
interpretation. No numerical value becomes a Lean premise. Do not change
packet weights, add more primes or enlarge the screen after seeing its result.

## Current outcome and positive survivor

The [completed diagnostic](../2-fully-proven/computations/ccm-fu-binary-gcd-compensation-2026-09-07/README.md)
finds 59 positive packets among all 2,550. At the first, M=11 and r=1,
independent 80-digit source reconstruction gives
`J_1=0.0038387660052104776300...>0`, while the complete cross sum is
`-0.0545935145526144963903...<0`. The proposed universal packet sign is
therefore rejected at the numerical-evidence level. No formal negative
theorem or route retirement is claimed.

The positive survivor is the complete source compensation: at this witness,
the negative gcd-three and gcd-five terms pay the residual positive binary
packet. The full strict diagonal ceiling is already formal as
`sum_mobiusDivisorGcdCross_eleven_lt_neg_oneHundredth`. It was not re-audited.

A second algebraic pass identifies the exact omitted reserve. With the four
paired odd cofactors `V_d=C_d+C_(2d)`, d=1,3,5,7, write
`H=2*sum_(d<e) V_d*V_e`. Pairwise coprimality of these four indices gives
`J_1=H+2*C_1*C_2`, whereas the complete cross sum is
`H+2*(C_1*C_2+C_3*C_6+C_5*C_10)`. These paper identities retain the actual
source. They show why the complete first-prime reserve cannot be assigned
only to its primitive gcd packet. The new packet positivity and this exact
paired decomposition are not Lean certificates; the already formal complete
source ceiling is the audited surviving positive statement.

This attempt does not establish a sharper full signed bound. Its next
arithmetic obligation is a joint comparison using all released pair terms,
rather than another claim that each fixed gcd packet has a separate sign.

o such estimate
was located by the corpus searches `Estermann`, `"continued fraction"
moebius`, and `cotangent cancellation`, or established in this attack.
No formalization of the external estimate is started without an argument
that also handles its missing balanced range and carrier comparison.

## Coprime complete-column cancellation: formalized arithmetic bound

The proved estimate uses the actual Möbius signs before taking absolute values.
For positive n, finite divisor inversion gives

`sum_(e|n, gcd(d,e)=1) mu(e) = [every prime dividing n divides d]`.

Let S(d,R) count positive n<=R supported on the primes of d. For alpha,delta>0,
Rankin's inequality and the finite prime Euler product give

`S(d,R) <= R^alpha * prod_(p|d)(1-p^(-alpha))^(-1)
          <= C_(alpha,delta) R^alpha d^delta`.

The second inequality is uniform in d: beyond a fixed prime threshold the
geometric factor is at most p^delta; the finite small-prime product is the
constant, and the product of distinct prime divisors divides d. Thus the
complete inner floor sum `sum_(e<=R, gcd(d,e)=1)mu(e)*floor(R/e)` is exactly
S(d,R), with subpower growth in both parameters.

Consequently, for every epsilon>0 the mixed floor correlation

`sum_(d<=N) mu(d)*floor(R/d) *
    sum_(e<=R, gcd(d,e)=1) mu(e)*floor(R/e)`

has absolute value at most C_epsilon R^(1+epsilon), uniformly in N. Indeed
terms d>R vanish, the support bound gives a harmonic sum, and its logarithm
is absorbed into a further arbitrarily small power. The same absolute
majorant applies when the outer divisors are restricted to N<d<=R.
This is a quantitative cancellation estimate for a component of the
arithmetic expansion, not an RH assumption or a norm-transfer theorem.

The full two-cutoff form still has an unpaid term. Split each complete divisor
sum into d<=N and d>N. The complete form and the two mixed terms can use the
preceding estimate; the term with both d>N and e>N keeps both Möbius signs
and the coprimality constraint and has no such complete-column inversion.
Residue/harmonic compensation must also stay paired in the actual energy.
`EulerDeletionCoprimeColumnCancellation` proves this estimate uniformly over
every finite outer divisor selection, including outer cutoffs and outer tails.
Its `complete_floor_column` proves the exact support-count identity;
`exists_floorCorrelation_le` supplies the unconditional quantitative bound.
These are statements about the explicit coprime floor correlation, not an
identification of that correlation alone with the full weighted EDQ energy.

The raw complementary double tail cannot have the desired smaller bound.
At cutoff one, let T(R) have both divisor ranges restricted to 2..R, and let
F(R) be the complete correlation. For every positive R, Lean proves
`T(R)=R^2-2*R+F(R)` and
`|T(R)-R^2+2*R|<=C_epsilon*R^(1+epsilon)`.
The positive survivor is the exact polynomial and its controlled remainder.
The active target is therefore the compensated double tail at growing
cutoffs, retaining the actual residue/harmonic terms and infinite energy
tail. A raw-tail subpower target would discard the polynomial exposed here.

[Full theorem statements and validation](../3-formalized/edq-coprime-column-cancellation.md).
The complete scratch, single-leaf build, and audit of eleven new public
declarations passed. Current repository lint passes.
No numerical experiment was needed for these algebraically forced facts.
The frontier map is read-only under the current user instruction.

## Active direct attack: exact common-divisor groups of the compensated Gram

The actual carrier has residue coordinates
`F(k)=sum_(d<=M) a(d)*(k mod d)/d`, with the literal raw or tapered coefficients.
Completing unweighted floor columns does not remove these normalized residues.

# EDQ complete-period residue covariance

Stage: 3-formalized. [BRIDGE] derived theorem; paper proof and Lean proof complete.
Full chain: Euler deletion → exact complex zero balance → signed arithmetic separation → off-line exclusion → RH.

The missing source comparison concerns the complete signed modular Gram. This
bridge isolates what exact period averaging preserves, before using any weighted
chronological estimate. It does not replace the missing cofinal logarithmic ceiling.

## Dependency-closed paper derivation

For a positive modulus m define c_m(k)=(k mod m)-(m-1)/2. Over every common
positive period P of m and n,

    sum_(k<P) c_m(k)c_n(k) = P*(gcd(m,n)^2-1)/12.

Write m=g*a, n=g*b with g=gcd(m,n) and a,b coprime. At k=g*j+i, 0<=i<g,
the centered residues are g*c_a(j)+c_g(i) and g*c_b(j)+c_g(i).
Chinese remaindering makes the a- and b-residue coordinates independent over
ab indices. Each has zero sum, so their conditional product sum is ab*c_g(i)^2.
The elementary square moment is sum_(i<g)c_g(i)^2=g*(g^2-1)/12.
Repetition gives every common period, with no limiting interchange.

Consequently, for any real coefficients u_m on positive moduli dividing P, the
period mean of sum_m u_m*(k mod m)/m is
sum_m u_m*(m-1)/(2m), and its centered second moment is exactly

    (1/12)*sum_(m,n) u_m*u_n*(gcd(m,n)^2-1)/(m*n).

The literal Möbius primitive therefore has mean (M_N-H_N)/2 and the corresponding
complete signed gcd-square covariance. Both Möbius signs and all common factors
remain present. The full second moment is mean squared plus this covariance.

For each residue r modulo P let

    W_P(r)=sum_(j>=0) 1/((r+P*j)*(r+P*j+1)),

with the zero-index summand equal to zero. The actual squared modular carrier
norm is exactly sum_(r mod P) abs(A_N(r))^2*W_P(r). Genuine summability and
periodicity justify this reindexing of the complete infinite series. The weights
are retained individually, including every nonzero multiple in the zero residue.

## Boundary of the result

These are complete-period identities. The existing carrier norm uses the
nonconstant weight 1/(k(k+1)); its full energy cannot be replaced by a period
average without controlling the resulting weighted remainder. The period may
grow extremely rapidly with the channel cutoff. No logarithmic energy ceiling,
source-current annihilation, off-line zero, or RH conclusion is asserted.

## Corpus and scientific-method audit

The existing coprime-period factorization supplies the CRT step. The reflected
logarithmic Gram controls the increment covariance gcd(m,n)-1, but does not
identify the covariance of the residue primitives. The existing Gram-residue
decomposition handles individual diagonals with their exact progression weights.
The common-divisor Abel cross decomposition retains masks for a different source.
None of these supplies the claimed primitive pair moment directly.

This is a derived [BRIDGE] under docs/meta/scientific-method.md, not a new primary
conjecture. The displayed result is predicted by the paper proof, so no numerical
experiment is justified or planned. The original RH objective remains unchanged.

/--
`norm_num` normalizes numerical expressions in the goal. By default, it supports the operations
`+` `-` `*` `/` `⁻¹` `^` and `%` over types with (at least) an `AddMonoidWithOne` instance, such as
`ℕ`, `ℤ`, `ℚ`, `ℝ`, `ℂ`. In addition to evaluating numerical expressions, `norm_num` will use `simp`
to simplify the goal. If the goal has the form `A = B`, `A ≠ B`, `A < B` or `A ≤ B`, where `A` and
`B` are numerical expressions, `norm_num` will try to close it. It also has a relatively simple
primality prover (available if you import `Mathlib.Tactic.NormNum.Prime`).

This tactic is extensible. Extensions can allow `norm_num` to evaluate more kinds of expressions, or
to prove more kinds of propositions (such as, primality of natural numbers). See the `@[norm_num]`
attribute for further information on extending `norm_num`.

* `norm_num at l` normalizes at location(s) `l`.
* `norm_num [h1, ...]` adds the arguments `h1, ...` to the `simp` set in addition to the default
  `simp` set. All options for `simp` arguments are supported, in particular `←`, `↑` and `↓`.
* `norm_num only` does not use the default `simp` set for simplification. `norm_num only [h1, ...]`
  uses only the arguments `h1, ...` in addition to the routines tagged `@[norm_num]`.
  `norm_num only` still performs post-processing steps, like `simp only`, use `norm_num1` if you
  exclusively want to normalize numerical expressions.
* `norm_num (config := cfg)` uses `cfg` as configuration for `simp` calls (see the `simp` tactic for
  further details).

Examples:
```lean
example : 43 ≤ 74 + (33 : ℤ) := by norm_num
example : ¬ (7-2)/(2*3) ≥ (1:ℝ) + 2/(3^2) := by norm_num
```
-/

/-
# Scalar bookkeeping for named analytic-method scenarios

`Method` stores an arbitrary family label and rational exponent. Its named instances are
calibration records; they contain no exponential sum or proof of an analytic estimate.
The inequalities below compare those records, not every possible method in either family.
Likewise the assigned `True`/`False` flags encode a scenario rather than proving properties
of an arithmetic source. Rational formulas later in the file have the same bookkeeping scope.

Historical declaration names are retained. Their theorem types, not their names, determine
what is proved. In particular this module does not establish an exhaustive method taxonomy,
a family-wide impossibility theorem, or an analytic implication from zero-freeness.
See `docs/drafts/pipeline/1-in-progress/corpus-method-model-semantics-audit.md`.
-/
import GaloisForLFunctions.HTGeometry.CorrelationExponentBridge

namespace HTGeometry

/-- Two labels used by the bookkeeping records; not an exhaustive classification of methods. -/
inductive ToolFamily
  | smooth
  | multiplicative
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

/-- An assigned family label and rational exponent, with no analytic estimate attached. -/
structure Method where
  family : ToolFamily
  savingExponent : ℚ

/-- Recorded smooth-labelled calibration with saving exponent `1/6`. -/
def vanDerCorputMethod : Method := ⟨ToolFamily.smooth, 1/6⟩

/-- Recorded smooth-labelled calibration with saving exponent `1 - 17/21`. -/
def bourgainMethod : Method := ⟨ToolFamily.smooth, 1 - 17/21⟩

/-- Recorded multiplicative-labelled calibration with saving exponent zero. -/
def halaszMethod : Method := ⟨ToolFamily.multiplicative, 0⟩

/-- A second recorded multiplicative-labelled calibration with saving exponent zero. -/
def amplificationMethod : Method := ⟨ToolFamily.multiplicative, 0⟩

/-- Assigned target saving `1/2` in this exponent model. -/
def lindelofSaving : ℚ := 1/2

@[simp] theorem bourgain_saving : bourgainMethod.savingExponent = 4/21 := by
  unfold bourgainMethod; norm_num

/-- Both named multiplicative calibration records have their assigned zero exponent. -/
theorem multiplicative_family_zero :
    halaszMethod.savingExponent = 0 ∧ amplificationMethod.savingExponent = 0 := by
  constructor <;> rfl

/-- The named Bourgain calibration lies below the assigned target. -/
theorem smooth_family_short : bourgainMethod.savingExponent < lindelofSaving := by
  rw [bourgain_saving]; unfold lindelofSaving; norm_num

/-- Three named calibration records lie below the assigned target; no family-wide quantifier occurs. -/
theorem neither_family_suffices :
    bourgainMethod.savingExponent < lindelofSaving ∧
    halaszMethod.savingExponent < lindelofSaving ∧
    amplificationMethod.savingExponent < lindelofSaving := by
  refine ⟨smooth_family_short, ?_, ?_⟩
  · unfold halaszMethod lindelofSaving; norm_num
  · unfold amplificationMethod lindelofSaving; norm_num

/-- The sum of the two displayed calibration exponents lies below the assigned target. -/
theorem families_do_not_add_up :
    bourgainMethod.savingExponent + halaszMethod.savingExponent < lindelofSaving := by
  rw [bourgain_saving]
  unfold halaszMethod lindelofSaving
  norm_num

/-- Difference between the assigned target and named Bourgain calibration. -/
@[simp] theorem best_shortfall : lindelofSaving - bourgainMethod.savingExponent = 13/42 := by
  rw [bourgain_saving]; unfold lindelofSaving; norm_num

/-- A proposed interface whose joint-use flags and target exponent are supplied as fields. -/
structure JointMethod where
  usesSmooth : Prop
  usesMultiplicative : Prop
  savingExponent : ℚ
  both : usesSmooth ∧ usesMultiplicative
  reaches : savingExponent = lindelofSaving

/-- The exponent is below target when the record is one of the three explicitly listed examples. -/
theorem no_single_family_is_joint (m : Method)
    (h : m = bourgainMethod ∨ m = halaszMethod ∨ m = amplificationMethod) :
    m.savingExponent < lindelofSaving := by
  rcases h with rfl | rfl | rfl
  · exact smooth_family_short
  · unfold halaszMethod lindelofSaving; norm_num
  · unfold amplificationMethod lindelofSaving; norm_num

parameter `x`. -/

theorem afeSaving_convexity {x : ℚ} (hx : x ≠ 1/2) : afeSaving (1/4) x = 1 := by
  unfold afeSaving
  have h : (1:ℚ)/2 - x ≠ 0 := by
    intro hc; apply hx; linarith
  rw [div_eq_one_iff_eq h]
  ring

def afeSavingSlopeNumerator (theta : ℚ) : ℚ := 2 * theta - 1/2

/-!
# Normed division rings and fields

In this file we define normed fields, and (more generally) normed division rings. We also prove
some theorems about these definitions.

Some useful results that relate the topology of the normed field to the discrete topology include:
* `norm_eq_one_iff_ne_zero_of_discrete`

Methods for constructing a normed field instance from a given real absolute value on a field are
given in:
* AbsoluteValue.toNormedField
-/

@[expose] public section

-- Guard against import creep.
assert_not_exists AddChar comap_norm_atTop DilationEquiv Finset.sup_mul_le_mul_sup_of_nonneg
  IsOfFinOrder Isometry.norm_map_of_map_one NNReal.isOpen_Ico_zero Rat.norm_cast_real
  RestrictScalars

variable {G α β ι : Type*}

open Filter
open scoped Topology NNReal ENNReal

/-- A normed division ring is a division ring endowed with a seminorm which satisfies the equality
`‖x y‖ = ‖x‖ ‖y‖`. -/
class NormedDivisionRing (α : Type*) extends Norm α, DivisionRing α, MetricSpace α where
  /-- The distance is induced by the norm. -/
  dist_eq : ∀ x y, dist x y = norm (-x + y)
  /-- The norm is multiplicative. -/
  protected norm_mul : ∀ a b, norm (a * b) = norm a * norm b

-- see Note [lower instance priority]
attribute [instance 10] NormedDivisionRing.toDivisionRing

-- see Note [lower instance priority]
/-- A normed division ring is a normed ring. -/
instance (priority := 100) NormedDivisionRing.toNormedRing [β : NormedDivisionRing α] :
    NormedRing α :=
  { β with norm_mul_le a b := (NormedDivisionRing.norm_mul a b).le }

-- see Note [lower instance priority]
/-- The norm on a normed division ring is strictly multiplicative. -/
instance (priority := 100) NormedDivisionRing.toNormMulClass [NormedDivisionRing α] :
    NormMulClass α where
  norm_mul := NormedDivisionRing.norm_mul

section NormedDivisionRing

variable [NormedDivisionRing α] {a b : α}

instance (priority := 900) NormedDivisionRing.to_normOneClass : NormOneClass α :=
  ⟨mul_left_cancel₀ (mt norm_eq_zero.1 (one_ne_zero' α)) <| by rw [← norm_mul, mul_one, mul_one]⟩

@[simp]
theorem norm_div (a b : α) : ‖a / b‖ = ‖a‖ / ‖b‖ :=
  map_div₀ (normHom : α →*₀ ℝ) a b

@[simp]
theorem nnnorm_div (a b : α) : ‖a / b‖₊ = ‖a‖₊ / ‖b‖₊ :=
  map_div₀ (nnnormHom : α →*₀ ℝ≥0) a b

theorem norm_inv (a : α) : ‖a⁻¹‖ = ‖a‖⁻¹ :=
  map_inv₀ (normHom : α →*₀ ℝ) a

@[simp]
theorem nnnorm_inv (a : α) : ‖a⁻¹‖₊ = ‖a‖₊⁻¹ :=
  NNReal.eq <| by simp

@[simp]
lemma enorm_inv {a : α} (ha : a ≠ 0) : ‖a⁻¹‖ₑ = ‖a‖ₑ⁻¹ := by simp [enorm, ENNReal.coe_inv, ha]

/-- The double large sieve is efficient only when this product is `≤ 0` in exponent. -/
theorem sieve_inefficient : 0 < sieveEfficiencyProduct := by
  unfold sieveEfficiencyProduct; norm_num

/-- Output exponent of the raw double large sieve. -/
def doubleSieveOutput : ℚ := 2/3

/-- **It is worse than the trivial bound by `N^{1/3}`.** -/
theorem doubleSieve_worse_than_trivial : bilinearTrivial < doubleSieveOutput := by

@[simp] theorem doubleSieve_deficit : doubleSieveOutput - bilinearTrivial = 1/3 := by
  unfold doubleSieveOutput bilinearTrivial; norm_num

/-- Points per box after subdividing to restore efficiency, as an exponent of `N`: `1/2 − 5/6`. -/
def pointsPerBox : ℚ := 1/2 - 5/6

/-- **Fewer than one point per box: the sieve degenerates under subdivision.** -/
theorem subdivision_degenerates : pointsPerBox < 0 := by
  unfold pointsPerBox; norm_num

/-- **The raw double large sieve is inapplicable here**, and the deficit it must overcome is `N^{1/3}`
— which is precisely what Bombieri–Iwaniec's spacing analysis supplies. -/
theorem raw_double_sieve_inapplicable :
    0 < sieveEfficiencyProduct ∧ bilinearTrivial < doubleSieveOutput ∧ pointsPerBox < 0 :=
  ⟨sieve_inefficient, doubleSieve_worse_than_trivial, subdivision_degenerates⟩


/-!
### Recalibration: progress measured from the raw sieve

On the normalised sum of Theorem 82 (exponents in `L = N^{1/3}`):

    raw double large sieve   :  L²          (Theorem 87)
    trivial bound            :  L¹
    Bourgain's record        :  L^{13/14}   (since `L^{3/2}·L^{13/14} = L^{17/7} = N^{17/21}`)
    Lindelöf                 :  L^{o(1)}

Measured from the **trivial** bound the record has covered `1 − 13/14 = 1/14 ≈ 7 %` of the way to
Lindelöf.  Measured from the **raw sieve** — the actual starting point of the Bombieri–Iwaniec method,
before any spacing analysis — it has covered

    (2 − 13/14) / 2  =  (15/14)/2  =  **15/28 ≈ 53.6 %** .

The discrepancy is exactly the factor `L` by which the raw sieve is worse than trivial: the spacing
analysis first has to climb back to the trivial bound, and only then begins to save.
-/

/-- Normalised-sum exponent (in `L`) of the raw double large sieve. -/
def normRawSieve : ℚ := 2

/-- Normalised-sum exponent of the trivial bound. -/
def normTrivial : ℚ := 1

/-- Normalised-sum exponent of Bourgain's record. -/
def normBourgain : ℚ := 13/14

/-- Normalised-sum exponent of the Lindelöf hypothesis. -/
def normLindelof : ℚ := 0

/-- **Bourgain's record restores to `N^{17/21}`.** -/
@[simp] theorem normBourgain_restores : (3/2 : ℚ) + normBourgain = 17/7 := by
  unfold normBourgain; norm_num

/-- Progress measured from the trivial bound. -/
def progressFromTrivial : ℚ := (normTrivial - normBourgain) / (normTrivial - normLindelof)

@[simp] theorem progressFromTrivial_eq : progressFromTrivial = 1/14 := by
  unfold progressFromTrivial normTrivial normBourgain normLindelof; norm_num

/-- Progress measured from the raw sieve. -/
def progressFromRawSieve : ℚ := (normRawSieve - normBourgain) / (normRawSieve - normLindelof)

@[simp] theorem progressFromRawSieve_eq : progressFromRawSieve = 15/28 := by
  unfold progressFromRawSieve normRawSieve normBourgain normLindelof; norm_num

/-- **From the raw sieve, more than half the required saving has been achieved.** -/
theorem majority_achieved_from_raw : 1/2 < progressFromRawSieve := by
  rw [progressFromRawSieve_eq]; norm_num

/-- **And the two measures differ by the factor `L` separating the raw sieve from trivial.** -/
theorem baselines_differ : progressFromTrivial < progressFromRawSieve := by
  rw [progressFromTrivial_eq, progressFromRawSieve_eq]; norm_num

/-- The remaining saving, from the record to Lindelöf. -/
@[simp] theorem remaining_saving : normBourgain - normLindelof = 13/14 := by
  unfold normBourgain normLindelof; norm_num

/-- **The duality law.**  The distance from a vector to the span of a family is the norm of its component
orthogonal to that span. -/
theorem infDist_span_eq_norm_starProjection_orthogonal (S : Set H) (x : H) :
    Metric.infDist x (Submodule.span 𝕜 S : Set H)
      = ‖(Submodule.span 𝕜 S)ᗮ.starProjection x‖ := by
  set K := Submodule.span 𝕜 S with hKdef
  set P := Kᗮ.starProjection x with hPdef
  have hPmem : P ∈ Kᗮ := Submodule.starProjection_apply_mem _ x
  have hsub : x - P ∈ Kᗮᗮ := Submodule.sub_starProjection_mem_orthogonal x
  have hclos : x - P ∈ K.topologicalClosure := by
    rwa [Submodule.orthogonal_orthogonal_eq_closure] at hsub
  refine le_antisymm ?_ ?_
  · have h1 : Metric.infDist x (K.topologicalClosure : Set H) ≤ ‖P‖ := by
      have h := Metric.infDist_le_dist_of_mem (x := x) (SetLike.mem_coe.2 hclos)
      rwa [dist_eq_norm, sub_sub_cancel] at h
    rwa [Submodule.topologicalClosure_coe, Metric.infDist_closure] at h1
  · rcases eq_or_ne P 0 with h0 | hne
    · rw [h0, norm_zero]
      exact Metric.infDist_nonneg
    · have hppos : 0 < ‖P‖ := norm_pos_iff.mpr hne
      have hbound := norm_inner_le_norm_mul_infDist_span S x P
        ((mem_orthogonal_span_iff S P).1 hPmem)
      rw [inner_starProjection_orthogonal_self K x, RCLike.norm_ofReal,
        abs_of_nonneg (by positivity : (0 : ℝ) ≤ ‖P‖ ^ 2), sq] at hbound
      exact le_of_mul_le_mul_left hbound hppos

/-- **The bound is attained.**  Some vector orthogonal to the family, of norm at most one, pairs with the
target exactly at the distance: the detector method is exact. -/
theorem exists_detector_norm_inner_eq_infDist_span (S : Set H) (x : H) :
    ∃ w : H, (∀ s ∈ S, inner 𝕜 w s = 0) ∧ ‖w‖ ≤ 1 ∧
      ‖inner 𝕜 w x‖ = Metric.infDist x (Submodule.span 𝕜 S : Set H) := by
  set K := Submodule.span 𝕜 S with hKdef
  set P := Kᗮ.starProjection x with hPdef
  have hPmem : P ∈ Kᗮ := Submodule.starProjection_apply_mem _ x
  have hperp : ∀ s ∈ S, inner 𝕜 P s = 0 := (mem_orthogonal_span_iff S P).1 hPmem
  have hdual : Metric.infDist x (K : Set H) = ‖P‖ :=
    infDist_span_eq_norm_starProjection_orthogonal S x
  rcases eq_or_ne P 0 with h0 | hne
  · refine ⟨0, by simp, by simp, ?_⟩
    rw [hdual, h0, norm_zero, inner_zero_left, norm_zero]
  · have hppos : 0 < ‖P‖ := norm_pos_iff.mpr hne
    have hcne : ((‖P‖⁻¹ : ℝ) : 𝕜) ≠ 0 := by
      simp only [ne_eq, RCLike.ofReal_eq_zero, inv_eq_zero]
      exact ne_of_gt hppos
    refine ⟨((‖P‖⁻¹ : ℝ) : 𝕜) • P, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
    · intro s hs
      rw [inner_smul_left, hperp s hs, mul_zero]
    · rw [norm_smul, RCLike.norm_ofReal, abs_of_pos (by positivity : (0 : ℝ) < ‖P‖⁻¹),
        inv_mul_cancel₀ (ne_of_gt hppos)]
    · rw [inner_smul_left, inner_starProjection_orthogonal_self K x, RCLike.conj_ofReal,
        norm_mul, RCLike.norm_ofReal, RCLike.norm_ofReal,
        abs_of_pos (by positivity : (0 : ℝ) < ‖P‖⁻¹),
        abs_of_nonneg (by positivity : (0 : ℝ) ≤ ‖P‖ ^ 2), hdual, sq, ← mul_assoc,
        inv_mul_cancel₀ (ne_of_gt hppos), one_mul]

/-- **Approximability is the nonexistence of a detector.** -/
theorem infDist_span_eq_zero_iff (S : Set H) (x : H) :
    Metric.infDist x (Submodule.span 𝕜 S : Set H) = 0
      ↔ ∀ w : H, (∀ s ∈ S, inner 𝕜 w s = 0) → inner 𝕜 w x = 0 := by
  refine ⟨fun h w hw => ?_, fun h => ?_⟩
  · have hb := norm_inner_le_norm_mul_infDist_span S x w hw
    rw [h, mul_zero] at hb
    exact norm_eq_zero.1 (le_antisymm hb (norm_nonneg _))
  · obtain ⟨w, hw, -, heq⟩ := exists_detector_norm_inner_eq_infDist_span (𝕜 := 𝕜) S x
    rw [← heq, h w hw, norm_zero]

/-- **Membership in a topological closure, dually.**  A vector lies in the closure of a subspace iff every
vector orthogonal to the subspace is orthogonal to it. -/
theorem mem_topologicalClosure_iff (K : Submodule 𝕜 H) (x : H) :
    x ∈ K.topologicalClosure ↔ ∀ w ∈ Kᗮ, inner 𝕜 w x = 0 := by
  rw [← Submodule.orthogonal_orthogonal_eq_closure, Submodule.mem_orthogonal]

/-- **Density, dually.**  A subspace is dense iff no nonzero vector is orthogonal to it. -/
theorem topologicalClosure_eq_top_iff (K : Submodule 𝕜 H) :
    K.topologicalClosure = ⊤ ↔ ∀ w ∈ Kᗮ, w = 0 := by
  rw [← Submodule.orthogonal_orthogonal_eq_closure]
  refine ⟨fun h w hw => ?_, fun h => ?_⟩
  · have hmem : w ∈ Kᗮᗮ := h ▸ Submodule.mem_top
    exact inner_self_eq_zero.1 (Submodule.inner_right_of_mem_orthogonal hw hmem)
  · have hbot : Kᗮ = ⊥ := by
      rw [eq_bot_iff]
      intro w hw
      exact (Submodule.mem_bot 𝕜).2 (h w hw)
    rw [hbot, Submodule.bot_orthogonal_eq_top]

/-
The van der Corput derivative tests, indexed by order, and the optimality of the third.

The classical `k`-th derivative test corresponds to the exponent pair

    **(κ_k, λ_k) = ( 1/(2^k - 2) ,  1 - (k-1)/(2^k - 2) )** ,   `k ≥ 3` ,

which is exactly the tower produced by iterating the `A`-process from `B(0,1)`, with `k = j + 2`.  So
the closed form obtained earlier from the `A`-recursion is the classical one, an independent
confirmation.

Its subconvexity exponent is

    **μ_k = 1/4 - (k-2) / (2(2^k - 2))** ,

which equals `1/6` at `k = 3` — Weyl's exponent — and **increases** with `k` toward the convexity
bound `1/4`:

    k = 3 : **1/6 = 0.166667** ,   k = 4 : **5/28 = 0.178571** ,
    k = 5 : **1/5 = 0.2** ,        k = 6 : **27/124 = 0.217742** .

So **the third derivative test is the best of the family at the critical line**, and every
higher-order test is strictly worse there — while, by the earlier scale analysis, the higher tests are
the ones that clear the small block scales.  That is the classical reason Weyl's `1/6` was the
baseline for sixty-five years: no order of van der Corput's method improves it.
-/
import GaloisForLFunctions.HTGeometry.ClassDecompositionNotAReduction

namespace HTGeometry

/-! ### The tests, indexed by order -/

/-- Denominator `2^k - 2` of the `k`-th derivative test. -/
def testDen (k : ℕ) : ℚ := 2 ^ k - 2

/-- First coordinate of the `k`-th test's exponent pair. -/
def testKappa (k : ℕ) : ℚ := 1 / testDen k

/-- Second coordinate. -/
def testLambda (k : ℕ) : ℚ := 1 - (k - 1) / testDen k

/-- Its subconvexity exponent. -/
def testMu (k : ℕ) : ℚ := 1 / 4 - (k - 2) / (2 * testDen k)

/-- **The `k`-th test is the `(k-2)`-nd member of the `A`-tower.** -/
theorem test_is_tower (j : ℕ) :
    testDen (j + 2) = towerDen j ∧ testKappa (j + 2) = towerKappa j := by
  constructor
  · unfold testDen towerDen; norm_num
  · unfold testKappa towerKappa
    congr 1

/-- And the second coordinates agree. -/
theorem test_lambda_is_tower (j : ℕ) : testLambda (j + 2) = towerLambda j := by
  unfold testLambda towerLambda
  rw [(test_is_tower j).1]
  push_cast
  ring

/-- **The exponents agree too.** -/
theorem test_mu_is_tower (j : ℕ) : testMu (j + 2) = towerMu j := by
  unfold testMu towerMu
  rw [(test_is_tower j).1]
  push_cast
  ring

/-! ### Values -/

theorem testDen_values :
    testDen 3 = 6 ∧ testDen 4 = 14 ∧ testDen 5 = 30 ∧ testDen 6 = 62 := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩ <;> (unfold testDen; norm_num)

/-- **The third test is Weyl's.** -/
@[simp] theorem testMu_three : testMu 3 = 1 / 6 := by
  unfold testMu testDen; norm_num

@[simp] theorem testMu_four : testMu 4 = 5 / 28 := by
  unfold testMu testDen; norm_num

@[simp] theorem testMu_five : testMu 5 = 1 / 5 := by
  unfold testMu testDen; norm_num

@[simp] theorem testMu_six : testMu 6 = 27 / 124 := by
  unfold testMu testDen; norm_num

/-- **The exponents increase with the order.** -/
theorem testMu_increasing :
    testMu 3 < testMu 4 ∧ testMu 4 < testMu 5 ∧ testMu 5 < testMu 6 := by
  rw [testMu_three, testMu_four, testMu_five, testMu_six]
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

/-- **And stay below the convexity bound.** -/
theorem testMu_below_convexity : testMu 6 < 1 / 4 := by
  rw [testMu_six]; norm_num

/-! ### Optimality of the third test -/

/-- **Weyl's exponent is the best in the family.** -/
theorem third_test_optimal :
    testMu 3 < testMu 4 ∧ testMu 3 < testMu 5 ∧ testMu 3 < testMu 6 := by
  rw [testMu_three, testMu_four, testMu_five, testMu_six]
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

/-- **And it is Weyl's `1/6`, the pre-1986 baseline.** -/
theorem third_test_is_weyl : testMu 3 = weylKappa := by
  rw [testMu_three]; unfold weylKappa; rfl

/-- **The record lies strictly below the whole family**, which is why every improvement since Weyl has
come from outside van der Corput's method. -/
theorem record_below_family :
    bourgainTheta < testMu 3 ∧ bourgainTheta < testMu 4 ∧ bourgainTheta < testMu 5 := by
  rw [testMu_three, testMu_four, testMu_five]
  unfold bourgainTheta
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

/-- **Summary.**  The derivative tests form the `A`-tower; their critical-line exponents increase from
Weyl's `1/6` toward `1/4`; the third is optimal; and the record `13/84` lies below all of them. -/
theorem derivative_test_summary :
    testMu 3 = 1 / 6 ∧ testMu 3 < testMu 4 ∧ testMu 6 < 1 / 4 ∧ bourgainTheta < testMu 3 :=
  ⟨testMu_three, testMu_increasing.1, testMu_below_convexity, record_below_family.1⟩

end HTGeometry
